questiontext.text:
Which is the best summary of the proof above that \(m^2 - 1\) is a multiple of 3 whenever the integer \(m\) is not a multiple of 3?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

generalfeedback.text:
A good summary names the structure of the proof and its key step. The proof is by exhaustion: every integer that is not a multiple of 3 is 1 or 2 more than a multiple of 3, so there are two cases, and in each one the difference of two squares shows a factor of 3. That is the second option.

  • Checking \(m = 1, 2, 4, 5, 7\) gives evidence, not a proof: there are infinitely many integers that are not multiples of 3, and no list of values covers them all.

  • Factorising alone is not enough. A product of two integers need not be a multiple of 3 (\(2 \times 4 = 8\)); the cases are what show that one of the factors is a multiple of 3.

  • The multiples of 3 are not a case to prove: for \(m = 3\), \(m^2 - 1 = 8\), which is not a multiple of 3. The hypothesis rules those integers out.

questiondescription.text: This question is based on the example headed Example 5.1 (Using divisibility), with Solution 5.2, pp. 18-19, in Section 5 of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.

truefeedback.text: Checking particular values gives evidence, not a proof: there are infinitely many integers that are not multiples of 3, and no list of values covers them all. Look again at how the proof above deals with every one of them at once.

If \(m\) is a multiple of 3, then \(m^2 - 1\) is not a multiple of 3 (for \(m = 3\) it is 8). The statement is only about integers that are not multiples of 3, so the proof does not prove that case: the hypothesis rules it out.

falsefeedback.text: Being a product of two integers does not make a number a multiple of 3: \(2 \times 4 = 8\). The proof needs the cases to show that one of the factors is a multiple of 3.
